title: Kids Outlearn AI — and Nobody Knows Why
hook: A toddler masters a language from a few years of overheard chatter. A chatbot needs a large fraction of the written internet. Nobody can fully explain the gap.
key_points: For all of human history, only one thing could learn a language to full fluency: a child.
Four years after ChatGPT, machines can do it too — but by a wildly different route.
Children learn from a trickle of messy, in-person speech; LLMs need vast text corpora.
MIT Technology Review reports researchers still can't explain why kids are so much more efficient.
The gap is a clue that human learning uses something today's models don't have.
content_html: For as long as people have talked to each other, exactly one thing in the world could learn a human language to perfect fluency: a human child. As MIT Technology Review's Elise Cutts puts it, four short years after ChatGPT there are now two. But the two get there by wildly different routes — and the mismatch is one of the more interesting open puzzles in AI.
extra_html:
A child picks up a language from a comparatively tiny amount of input: fragmentary, error-filled, in-person chatter, spread over a few years, alongside learning to walk and eat with a spoon. A large language model needs a staggering volume of written text — far more words than any person could read in a lifetime. Both arrive at fluency; only one of them is remotely efficient about it.

Cutts reports that researchers still can't fully explain the gap. That's worth sitting with, because it cuts against a common assumption: that because AI now does something only humans could do, it must be doing it the way humans do. The efficiency difference suggests children bring something to the task — built-in structure, embodied experience, social feedback, or some combination — that scaling up text prediction doesn't replicate. It's also a reminder that "human-level performance" and "human-like learning" are separate claims, and only the first one is settled.

related.title: How AI Learns
related.hook: Training an AI is like teaching by flashcards on a massive scale: show it an example, let it guess, tell it how wrong it was, and nudge it to do better — billions of times.

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

related.title: Can AI Learn to Simulate the Real World?
related.hook: The next AI frontier isn't just predicting the next word — it's building an internal 'world model' that predicts what happens next in reality. Experts say it's promising, and still very unproven.

prereqs.title: How AI Learns
prereqs.hook: Training an AI is like teaching by flashcards on a massive scale: show it an example, let it guess, tell it how wrong it was, and nudge it to do better — billions of times.

flashcards.prompt: What's the biggest difference between how a child and an LLM learn language?

choices.text: The child learns fluently from a tiny amount of everyday speech; the model needs enormous amounts of text
The child memorizes a dictionary first, the model doesn't
The model learns from speech, the child learns from writing

flashcards.explanation_html: Both end up fluent, but a child gets there on a trickle of messy, in-person conversation, while a language model needs a vast written corpus.

flashcards.prompt: Why do researchers find children's language learning interesting for AI?
flashcards.back_html: Kids reach fluency on far less data than any model needs — a hint that human learning relies on something today's AI doesn't have.

flashcards.prompt: Does an AI matching a human skill mean it learned the way humans do?
flashcards.back_html: No. Same outcome, very different route — language models arrive at fluency by a method nothing in nature uses.
